title: I messed up and I don't know what to do now
blurb: For the hours after you blew up, went cold, or said the thing — when shame is loudest and the urge is to fix it immediately.
entry_signals: I said something I can't take back
I don't know how to face them
I need to apologise but I don't know what to say
I keep replaying what I did

steps.ask: Where are you right now, one to ten?
steps.help: Not how bad the thing was. How loud it is in you at this moment.

steps.title: Not from here
steps.say:
Two things go wrong at this level. Whatever you send will be written to make the feeling stop rather than to reach them — and afterwards you will not fully remember choosing it.

The repair does not expire. It survives a night. What does not survive is a message sent to get relief, which usually needs its own repair later.

Come back when it is quieter. If you need to send anything now, send only this: that you know something went wrong, and that you will come back to it properly.
cites: The Fawn Response After A Rupture

steps.ask: Before anything about patterns — was anyone frightened, hurt, or unsafe?
steps.help: This comes first on purpose. Everything below assumes a rupture between two people who can still talk. If it was more than that, the questions underneath are the wrong ones.

options.label: Yes — someone was frightened or hurt
It was ugly but nobody was frightened

steps.title: This needs more than a flow
steps.say:
If someone was frightened or hurt, that is not a communication problem and it is not something to work out alone at two in the morning with a set of questions.

That holds whichever side of it you are on. The thing that helps is a person — a therapist, a service, someone who can sit with the whole of it and is not inside the situation.

One thing worth carrying anyway: an explanation of where a reaction came from is not the same as a defence of what it did, and offering the first as though it settles the second is what usually makes these worse.
cites: Separating The Feeling From The Action

steps.say:
Start with something that will not feel like progress. You are here, aware that it went wrong, which is a different position from where this pattern usually runs — badly, and without noticing.

That is not absolution and it does not fix anything. It is the rung you are actually on, and the next one is only reachable from it.
steps.help: The reflex after catching yourself is usually a round of self-attack. It feels like accountability and it does none of accountability's work.

steps.ask: How urgent does apologising feel right now?
steps.help: Worth knowing before you do it, because urgency is information about you rather than about them.

options.label: Extremely — I can't settle until it's fixed
I want to, but I can wait
Honestly, I'd rather not have to

steps.say:
That pressure to resolve it immediately is not the repair. It is the same threat response that produced the rupture, pointed the other way — and it optimises for the relationship feeling safe again in the next ten minutes, not for the thing actually changing.

An apology delivered from there tends to over-promise, because over-promising is what makes the feeling stop fastest.
cites: The Fawn Response After A Rupture
An Apology Must Promise It Will Never Happen Again

steps.ask: Write down what actually happened. All of it, unfiltered — including the parts you would not want quoted.
steps.help: Not the version you would tell a friend, and not the version you would defend. Times, words, what you did. Read it as data rather than as a charge sheet. You cannot change something you have not been able to look at squarely.

steps.ask: Now the useful question. If the thing in front of you had been solved right then — would the feeling have stopped?
steps.help: Take it seriously rather than answering quickly. It is the cleanest test there is for what you were actually reacting to.

options.label: Yes — it was about what was happening
No — it would still have been there

cites: Insatiable Anger As A Trauma Signal

steps.say:
Then the size of it did not belong to this occasion, and no apology about this occasion will settle it — which is why these episodes repeat even after they are talked through.

That does not make what you did their problem, and it is not a reason to explain the history at them. It changes what you are apologising for: the way you handled it, which is yours, rather than the feeling, which is real and needs somewhere else to go.
cites: Responding To The Past In The Present
Separating The Feeling From The Action

steps.say: Then this is the more straightforward kind, which is genuinely good news — it means the repair can be about the actual thing.

steps.ask_a: What are you apologising for — the specific thing you did?
steps.ask_b: And what was the need or feeling underneath it that still needs somewhere to go?
steps.help_a: The action. Not the state that produced it. Specific enough that they would recognise it.
steps.help_b: Keep this. The instinct after a rupture is to disown the whole episode, feeling included — but the need does not stop existing because you expressed it badly.
cites: Separating The Feeling From The Action

steps.ask: Were you about to promise it will never happen again?
steps.help: No wrong answer. It is just worth catching before it is said out loud.

options.label: I was going to imply it

cites: An Apology Must Promise It Will Never Happen Again

steps.say:
A guarantee is the tempting shape, and it is the one that costs you their trust — because a pattern laid down early does not end after one bad night, so the promise is usually a lie, and a lie repeated across several apologies is what teaches someone not to believe you.

The version that holds has three parts: what you did and what you can see it cost them; that there is something in you still unresolved that this comes out of; and an actual conversation about what would make it less likely next time. Naming the unhealed thing is not a plea for leniency — it gives them enough of the picture to decide their own limits, which is what people are really asking for when they ask whether you have changed.

steps.ask: Last one, and it is about you rather than them. What will you do next time you feel that specific thing coming — not what you will stop feeling?
steps.help: Set it now while you are regulated, for a version of you who will not be. Leave the room, go for the walk, say you need an hour. Priebe's own is not continuing a conversation once anger passes a known threshold. She does not keep it perfectly. Imperfectly has still changed things.
cites: A Boundary With Your Own Triggered Self

steps.say:
What you have is the three-part apology and one thing you will do differently — both in your own words rather than mine.

One last thing, for when you deliver it. If they meet it with the ten other things you have not accounted for, that is worth expecting rather than being wounded by. You can hold that and say so, and still not withdraw the apology.
